hints: Focus on the total number of valence electrons in each molecule, as odd versus even tells you a lot about pairing.
Count them out: N brings 5, O brings 6 and H brings 1, so check the totals for NO, NO2 and NH3.
Remember that an odd total must leave one electron unpaired, while an even total can allow everything to pair up in bonds and lone pairs.
walkthrough:
**Use the odd-electron shortcut**

Think simply first. If a neutral molecule has an odd total number of valence electrons, they cannot all pair, so at least one must be unpaired. If the total is even, it is normally all paired.

Rule to use:
$$\text{odd total valence } e^- \rightarrow \text{radical, at least one unpaired } e^-$$

**Count valence electrons for 1 and 2**

Nitrogen is in Group 15 so it contributes 5 valence electrons, and oxygen in Group 16 contributes 6.

For $\text{NO}$:
$$5 + 6 = 11 \text{ (odd)}$$ 
So $\text{NO}$ must have an unpaired electron.

For $\text{NO}_2$:
$$5 + (2 \times 6) = 17 \text{ (odd)}$$ 
So $\text{NO}_2$ must also have an unpaired electron. This is why both are famous free radicals.

**Count valence electrons for 3 and conclude**

For $\text{NH}_3$, nitrogen brings 5 and each hydrogen brings 1:
$$5 + (3 \times 1) = 8 \text{ (even)}$$ 
In ammonia these 8 electrons form three N-H bonding pairs plus one lone pair on N, so all are paired.

Conclusion: 1 and 2 only are correct.

options.A: Incorrect. This would include 1, 2 and 3. While NO and NO2 are correct with odd electron counts of 11 and 17, NH3 has 8 valence electrons all paired in bonds and a lone pair, so it does not belong.
options.B: Correct. NO has 11 valence electrons and NO2 has 17 valence electrons. Both totals are odd, so each must contain an unpaired electron and behave as a radical. NH3 has 8 valence electrons, all paired.
options.C: Incorrect. This would include 2 and 3 only. NO2 is correctly included, but NH3 is wrongly included and NO is wrongly left out. NH3 is fully paired, while NO is a radical that should be included.
options.D: Incorrect. This would include 1 only. NO is indeed a radical, but this misses NO2 which also has an odd electron count of 17 and an unpaired electron. Both 1 and 2 are needed.
